tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: ccp is a teaching-scale but faithful build of an AI-native compliance automation platform: connectors land immutable raw events, normalization and identity resolution produce canonical entities, evaluators produce verdicts with verified citations, and a bitemporal state table answers both "what is true" and "what did we believe". The README lists the commands by area (migrate, load knowledge, run a tenant, report, evals, serve) and the two fixture tenants, acme and globex. spec.md (v1.3, seventeen layers) is the source of truth, and its running assumptions log (A-1 onward) explains why surprising choices were made, while the engineering review records the decision register that shaped the design. The tour follows one finding from raw evidence to a confirmed fix.

tour.title: Entry Points and Pipeline
tour.description: `python -m ccp` lands in __main__.py, which hands off to the Typer app in cli.py; cli.py mounts every sub-command (tenants, db, connectors, ingest, worker, evals, state, audit, aws and more), and each command opens a tenant-scoped database pool and delegates to a domain module. compliance_state/run.py is the best one-page map of the system: one idempotent run for a tenant ingests, normalizes, resolves identities, refreshes the retrieval index, drains evaluations and writes compliance state, which is the order the next steps follow. api/app.py is the other front door, the FastAPI /v1 API behind `ccp serve` that exposes onboarding, the approvals inbox, findings, fix suggestions, autonomy levels, method cards and the auditor workspace.
tour.languageLesson: A package's __main__.py runs when you execute `python -m package`, so a thin module that calls the Typer app gives one CLI both as a console script (pyproject.toml binds `ccp` to ccp.cli:app) and as a module. Typer builds nested command groups by mounting sub-apps with add_typer, which lets each domain package own its own commands.

tour.title: Tenant-Scoped Foundation
tour.description: Every later step relies on one invariant: tenant data is read only through ScopedDB (storage/scoped.py), which sets app.tenant_id inside each transaction so Postgres row-level security filters every row, and no method even accepts a tenant id. tenancy.py resolves the typed TenantContext and refuses suspended, offboarded or other-cell tenants, and config.py is the only module that reads the environment, which is why scoped.py and config.py have the highest fan-in in the codebase. db.py hardens the database roles (NOBYPASSRLS), applies the add-only migrations exactly once and provides the app, read-only agent and replica pools, while 0002_rls.sql shows the pattern each table follows: least-privilege grants plus FORCE row-level security with a tenant_isolation policy.
tour.languageLesson: Postgres row-level security attaches a policy predicate to every query on a table; FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies it even to the table owner, and a role created with NOBYPASSRLS cannot skip it. Setting a variable with SET LOCAL (or set_config(name, value, true)) scopes it to the current transaction, so a pooled connection never carries one tenant's id into the next request.

tour.title: Connectors Land Raw Evidence
tour.description: The pipeline starts with connectors, which all implement the contract in connectors/base.py: a SourceEvent keyed by the provider's own event id and timestamp, and a SyncReport that marks each declared scope complete, partial, not visible or failed, so a missing source is never mistaken for a pass. The AWS connector assumes the customer's onboarded read-only role and snapshots S3 public-access blocks, CloudTrail trails and IAM users, keeping each raw response with its request id; fixture connectors replay files such as acme's employees.json, where one employee terminated in August 2026 starts the leaver story this tour follows. landing.py writes every event into the immutable raw zone and the event log with deduplication and records each pull as a sync run, so one connector's failure never aborts the others. In production raw_zone.py keeps those objects in an Object-Locked S3 bucket with content digests and version ids, so any piece of evidence can be re-read and re-hashed later.
tour.languageLesson: Connector is a typing.Protocol: any class with matching methods satisfies it structurally, without inheriting from a base class. That is what lets the registry swap a fixture connector for a live one without the ingest code knowing the difference.

tour.title: Normalization and Identity
tour.description: Landed events flow through event_log.py, a Kafka-style queue kept in a Postgres table with per-tenant ordered sequence numbers, leased parallel claims, backoff, parking and dead letters; every later stage is a consumer of one of its topics. The normalize consumer reads each raw event back from the raw zone, runs the connector's pure mapper and persists canonical entities (Person, AccessGrant, Asset, Evidence and more) that carry provenance back to the raw event. Identity resolution then decides whether the HRIS leaver and a GitHub login are the same person: scoring.py applies a kind gate before computing any feature, so humans are never merged with service or shared accounts, and routes a weighted score to auto_merge, auto_distinct or review. resolver.py logs every decision, writes person links on auto-merge and sends uncertain pairs to the approval stage you will meet in Step 11.

tour.title: Verdicts and Bitemporal State
tour.description: Before seeing how a verdict is decided, it helps to know what one is and where it lands. verdict.py defines the Verdict and Citation schema shared by every evaluator tier, with an evaluation-key hash that makes retries no-ops and an insert stamped with the release bundle. 0005_state.sql creates the append-only verdicts table, which keeps the exact model request and response for replay, and the bitemporal compliance_state table, with UPDATE and DELETE revoked from the app role. bitemporal.py appends rows with valid time and transaction time and supersedes instead of updating, writer.py writes exactly one state row per verdict with its reason (correction, rule change, late event, new evidence), and reader.py answers current, believed and as-of questions plus the framework rollup.
tour.languageLesson: A bitemporal table tracks two timelines: valid time (when a fact was true in the world) and transaction time (when the system recorded it). Because rows are only appended and later rows supersede earlier ones, the same table answers 'what is true now' and 'what did we believe on date X', which is exactly what an auditor asks.

tour.title: Knowledge and Tier-1 Rules
tour.description: Every verdict is about a test in the knowledge catalogue: knowledge/graph.py defines Framework, Requirement, Control and TestSpec models with cross-reference validation and the tier router, and tests.yaml declares the fourteen tests (GH-1..5, HR-1..5, AWS-1..3, IDP-1) with their evidence types, controls and required complete sources. Tier 1 is deterministic code: gh1.py flags a person terminated in HRIS who still holds GitHub access observed after the termination, and returns needs_review instead of guessing when the identity link from Step 5 is still pending. Newer checks are declarative YAML, such as aws1.yaml, which requires the effective S3 public access block on every bucket, and declarative.py is the total interpreter that validates each check at load and applies it to the tenant's entities. New declarative checks can also be drafted offline by a model, but they reach the catalogue only through code gates and a named reviewer's accept.
tour.languageLesson: Pydantic models validate YAML-loaded data when it is loaded, so a malformed declarative check fails when the catalogue loads rather than in the middle of an evaluation. A 'total' interpreter returns a result (a verdict or an abstention) for every well-formed check, so no tenant data can crash it.

tour.title: Tier 2: Extract Then Rule
tour.description: Some evidence is prose, such as security-training records, so tier 2 lets a model read but keeps the decision in code. The evaluations consumer in evaluators/runner.py routes each record by tier, reuses stored verdicts and wraps the AI tiers with the daily model budget, the completeness guard and the second reader. tier2.py runs one hybrid retrieval (hybrid.py fuses Postgres full-text and pgvector arms by reciprocal rank fusion under row-level security), fences the evidence, makes one structured extraction call and verifies citations with citations.py, which nulls any field whose quote is not a contiguous run of words from a chunk the model was actually shown. A rule in code, here hr3.py, then decides PASS, PARTIAL, FAIL or needs_review from the verified fields, and confidence is computed in code rather than reported by the model.

tour.title: One Read-Only Tool Surface
tour.description: Before the agents, meet the only things they can touch. tools.py is a typed registry of read-only tools (evidence search and reading, access, state, verdicts, controls, rollups) closed over ScopedDB from Step 3, so no tool can cross tenants, and every call goes through one BoundTool gateway. allowlists.py gives each graph its own tool list and refuses off-list tools at build time, authz.py adds a default-deny policy check (permit, deny or ask) with operator rules from config/tool_policy.yaml and logs every decision, and prompt_guard.py is the single path for evidence and tool output into prompts, redacting secrets, flagging injection markers and wrapping content in random-nonce fences. rest.py exposes the same registry as /v1/tools through the same gateway and policy check, so people and agents share one surface.

tour.title: Agents That Only Propose
tour.description: The three agents are LangGraph graphs declared over one shared core: core.py supplies mandatory retry and timeout policies, structured extraction nodes, the bounded allowlisted tool loop with stop reasons and context ceilings, and citation-verification nodes with one correction round. The Investigator diagnoses a failing verdict and may only propose actions bounded to the fix catalogue, the Policy Agent searches only policy documents to report gaps or draft Markdown, and the Copilot answers operator questions; none of the three graphs has a write path. budget.py enforces hard caps on tokens, dollars, wall-clock time and tool calls inside every model client and raises RunStopped, so an operator's Stop takes effect without the agent's cooperation. Anything an agent wants done becomes a proposal for a person, which is where the next step picks up.
tour.languageLesson: LangGraph models an agent as a state graph: nodes are functions that read and return state, edges choose the next node, and a checkpointer persists state per thread. That persistence is what lets a run pause at an interrupt for a human decision and resume later from exactly where it stopped.

tour.title: The Human Approval Stage
tour.description: Agents and many code paths converge on one approval stage. approvals/store.py keeps approval items and their events append-only and authorizes decisions by role, requester separation and expiry (with audited admin break-glass), while actions.py defines what approving or rejecting means for each kind, from agent-run tier-3 interrupts and exceptions to the identity merges of Step 5 and tenant scope changes, failing closed on payloads the reviewer never saw. agent/decisions.py records each reviewer decision on a tier-3 interrupt together with a queued apply job in one transaction and audits decisions left unapplied. Newer drafting workflows land here too: the questionnaire pipeline maps each question to a tested control, derives its yes or no from current verdicts, drafts the answer with tool-less model steps over fenced evidence and stores it for approval in the inbox that ui.py renders.

tour.title: Suggest-Only Remediation
tour.description: When a test fails, CCP suggests a fix; it never opens pull requests or changes the customer's systems. lookups/runner.py first reads AWS Config history, CloudTrail events and the organization's Terraform for each failing resource and lands the responses as raw evidence; when the tier-1 rule already explains the failure, investigation/written.py writes the investigation in code with no model, and otherwise the Investigator from Step 10 chooses a fix by id. The fix comes from the versioned catalogue in fixes.yaml (S3 public access block, IAM console access and MFA, multi-region CloudTrail, GitHub collaborator removal), which remediation/fixes.py renders in code and checks offline for parameters, CLI safety, Terraform syntax and change scope before anyone sees it. The customer applies it, and confirm.py marks the suggestion confirmed only when a later read passes or no longer names the resource, and reopens it if it fails again within 30 days, so a person clicking accept never counts as proof.

tour.title: Evals, Method Cards and Autonomy
tour.description: Model-backed steps are measured rather than trusted. `ccp evals run` (evals/runner.py) runs golden and adversarial cases in a scratch database, k times for model-backed targets, and judge.py grades outputs against rubrics with the candidate fenced as untrusted data and checks for order and length bias. regress.py compares each run with the previous baseline (status flips, cost, attack success rate, p95 latency, Wilson bounds on false-PASS rates), and its exit code drives CI. publish.py turns these measurements into method cards that explain how a verdict or fix suggestion was decided and quarterly quality snapshots per workflow, and autonomy.py lets a workflow's drafts skip the Step 11 approval stage only on a published snapshot for the current release bundle, with a seeded review sample, a daily exposure budget and demotion when the bundle changes or quality alarms fire.

tour.title: Audit Chain, Packages and Observability
tour.description: An auditor needs proof that nothing was quietly rewritten. 0043_audit_chain.sql adds a per-tenant tamper-evident hash chain, appended by a deferred constraint trigger on 20 record tables, and audit/checkpoints.py signs each tenant's chain head and exports it write-once to an S3 Object Lock compliance-mode bucket. packages.py builds as-of audit packages from the bitemporal state of Step 6, with the method, raw evidence pointers, chain proofs and a signed manifest, and auditors.py gives named auditors time-boxed, read-only access to those packages, recording each grant as an attestation before it is made. Alongside this, observability/steps.py writes one masked JSON record per step with OpenTelemetry gen_ai attributes and model cost and mirrors it to Langfuse, whose failure never loses the local record.
tour.languageLesson: In a hash chain each entry stores the hash of the previous entry, so altering any row breaks every later link. A Postgres constraint trigger declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED runs at commit instead of after each statement, so the chain entry is computed once the transaction's rows are final.

tour.title: Deployment, Cells and Scale
tour.description: In production one container image runs both the `ccp serve` API and the `ccp worker run` worker as ECS Fargate services; the Dockerfile builds it on python:3.12-slim from the frozen uv lockfile and runs as a non-root user. deploy.yml gates every deploy on the CI checks plus a strict eval regression from Step 13, then pushes the image to ECR, runs `ccp db migrate` as a one-off Fargate task and rolls both services, with a manual rollback path. Scale comes in cells: cells.py resolves the cell a process serves, which fixes its region, data residency (such as the EU cell) and whether models are reached through the first-party API or regional Bedrock profiles. scale.tf adds a PgBouncer pool in transaction mode and an optional RDS read replica, and partitions.py moves the largest tenants into their own Postgres partitions while keeping forced row-level security and the tenant_isolation policy.
tour.languageLesson: PgBouncer in transaction mode hands a server connection to a client only for the length of one transaction, so session-level state such as SET (without LOCAL) or session prepared statements can leak to the next client or vanish. Scoping the tenant id to each transaction, as ScopedDB does in Step 3, is what keeps row-level security correct behind the pooler.
